title: Light to the Gentiles (Acts 13:13–52)
hook: a friend goes home, a sermon splits a city, and the chapter ends on joy
tomorrow: what do you do when a crowd tries to worship you?

segments.voice: Yesterday, a church at worship, hungry on purpose, and two friends set apart for a job. The line: while they worshiped.

Rejection emails tend to open politely: thank you so much for your interest. The no comes in the second paragraph. Paul and Barnabas get a few of those. At Perga, young John Mark leaves the team and goes home to Jerusalem, and Acts doesn't say why. The two push on to another Antioch, in Pisidia, and on the sabbath they sit down in the synagogue. After the reading of the law and the prophets, the leaders send them a friendly note: "Ye men and brethren, if ye have any word of exhortation for the people, say on." Paul stands up. By the end of the chapter, he'll be run out of the region, and the last word will be joy.
screen: `THANK YOU FOR YOUR INTEREST.` → `JOHN MARK GOES HOME.` → `SAY ON.`

segments.voice: Paul tells Israel's story, from Egypt to King David, then the story of Jesus, raised from the dead. The next sabbath "came almost the whole city together to hear the word of God." And the welcome splits. Many listeners, Jews and converts, follow Paul and Barnabas and want more. Others push back, and the talk turns sharp. So the two reach for a line from Isaiah: "I have set thee to be a light of the Gentiles, that thou shouldest be for salvation unto the ends of the earth." Notice where that line lives: in the scriptures read in that very synagogue. The hope of light for the nations is Israel's own prophet speaking. The Gentiles hear it and are glad. Then leading people of the city are stirred up, and Paul and Barnabas are driven out. They shake the dust off their feet and walk on to Iconium. And the chapter's last line: "And the disciples were filled with joy, and with the Holy Ghost." Here's what this gives you for a week with a no in it. Shaking off the dust doesn't pretend nothing happened; it admits the door closed. And Acts doesn't explain the joy, or say exactly which disciples it means. It just sets the dust and the joy side by side, and lets both be true.
screen: `THE WELCOME SPLITS.` · `A LIGHT OF THE GENTILES.` · `SHAKE OFF THE DUST.` · `DUST AND JOY, SIDE BY SIDE.` · then, large: `FILLED WITH JOY.`

segments.voice: Make a fist around one no you've had lately: a rejection, a cold shoulder, a plan that fell through. Hold it tight for a few breaths and feel it. Then open your hand, palm up, on your knee, and keep it open for the rest of the sit: the no still true, and room beside it.
Light to the Gentiles. Isaiah's line, spoken in Pisidian Antioch: a light for the nations, to the ends of the earth.
Your line: filled with joy, written right after the dust came off their feet. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Some churches sing Simeon's song, which calls Jesus a light to lighten the Gentiles, at evening prayer, and read Isaiah's light for the nations in the weeks around Christmas and Epiphany.

fork.setup: a friend didn't make the team she trained all year for, and keeps saying she's 'totally fine.' what fits today's ending?
options: let her be sad, and point to one good thing that's still true.
tell her real faith would make her joyful about it already.
change the subject until she stops thinking about it.
fork.reveal: Paul and Barnabas shook off the dust: the no was real. and the disciples were filled with joy anyway. Acts lets both stand.

notes: Written 2026-10-13 in the year-2-4 recipe (style pass and new-lesson data built in from the start).

Framing: Acts 13:45 and 13:50 name 'the Jews' as opposing Paul. The lesson says 'others push back' and 'leading people of the city are stirred up', and stresses that many Jews and converts followed (13:43) and that the light line is Isaiah's. Confirm this is fair and accurate.
Whether 'the disciples' in 13:52 are the travelers or the new believers is left open on purpose.
v3 life shape: the teach turns to 'a week with a no in it'; the reading of shaking off the dust as admitting the door closed is the lesson's own, offered gently. Confirm.
v3 myth item (the popular misreading): everyone in the synagogue turned on Paul. Acts 13:42–43 says otherwise.
